title: Share ideas and choose language for the occasion
intro: I can share turns, build on other people’s ideas and use language that suits our agreed way of working.
exampleTitle: Show that you heard the idea before adding yours
example: Asha says, “Let’s put the model bridge on a wide base so it will stand up.” Ben waits until she finishes, then says, “Your wide base could help it stand. Could we also add a support underneath?” Ben restates Asha’s point and adds a connected suggestion. He does not have to agree with every idea to work cooperatively. If the group has not agreed how to take turns, first ask, “How shall we make sure everyone can contribute?”
steps: 1. Share turns and check understanding

A conversation works when people understand how to join, finish and hand over a turn. Listen or attend to the whole contribution, then respond to its meaning. Invite a contribution without forcing someone to speak. A check such as “What will we do first?” gives better evidence of understanding than assuming everyone followed.

Model A: Jo says, “First we will label the pots; then we will add soil.” Lee waits and says, “So labels come before soil. Have I understood?” Jo confirms. Model B: Pat says, “I have finished my idea. Sam, would you like to add anything, or pass?” Sam chooses to pass. The group leaves space for Sam to contribute later. Both exchanges make the shared plan clearer.
Mira says, “Put the blue label on the empty tray before we fill it.” You did not hear which tray. What could you say next? Then suggest a question that checks the order of the jobs.

For example, “Which tray should have the blue label?” asks for the missing detail. “Do we label the tray before we fill it?” checks the order. Other relevant clear questions are valid. Give Mira time to answer; do not pretend you heard the missing information.
2. Match the occasion and the agreed roles

Formality is how the language and conventions fit an occasion and relationship. Familiar pair work may allow a quick request; a chaired meeting may have a named person who invites questions. Clear, respectful short words can suit both. For First Nations Australian events, check the roles and local guidance with the hosts; one community’s arrangements do not set rules for every community.

Pair work model: a friend has finished speaking, so Kim asks, “Can I add an idea?” Chaired school meeting model: the chair has asked students to wait to be invited; Kim signals in the agreed way, waits, then says, “Thank you. Could I ask how the groups will be chosen?” The difference is the shared convention, audience and role, not the length of the words. Reconciliation Australia explains that a Welcome to Country is delivered by Traditional Owners, or Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander people given permission by Traditional Owners; anyone can offer an Acknowledgement of Country. The purposes and roles differ. Follow checked local guidance rather than inventing ceremony words.

At this fictional visit, the host has specifically told your class, “Please save questions until I invite them. You can ask me afterwards if you prefer.” You have a question during the explanation. What could you do, and what could you ask the host if the arrangement is unclear?

Wait for the invitation or use the offered chance afterwards. If unsure, ask at an appropriate pause, “Could you explain when we may ask questions?” These are this host’s supplied directions, not a universal First Nations speaking rule. Check the actual host’s arrangements in a real visit. Do not assume that offering an Acknowledgement gives someone the role of delivering a Welcome.
3. Develop ideas together

Start a topic clearly, affirm a useful contribution, ask a relevant question and add a reason. To change topics, negotiate rather than abruptly taking over. Useful feedback names a specific feature and a possible improvement. Check both individual and group understanding before acting.

Model A: “Shall we decide how to label our display?” starts a topic. “Your large labels will be easy to read. Could we put each label beside its model?” affirms and builds. Model B: “I think the map needs a key because I cannot tell what the dots mean” gives specific feedback. “Have we finished discussing the map? Could we talk about the title next?” negotiates a change. “What will each of us do first?” checks the shared plan.

Noor says, “Let’s put all our labels at the bottom of the display.” You think visitors may not know which label belongs to each object. Give a respectful response with a reason and a suggestion. Then ask to move on to choosing the display title.

One response is “The labels will be together, but visitors may not know which object each one names. Could we put a label beside each object?” Then ask, “Have we finished deciding the labels? Shall we choose the title next?” Accept other relevant wording that explains the concern, offers a workable suggestion and lets the group respond. Agreement alone is not required.
mistakes: “Taking turns means everyone must speak immediately.”
Invite people and allow thinking time or a pass. Use the group’s agreed communication modes.
“Formal language must use long words.”
Clear, respectful words and the occasion’s agreed roles matter. A short question can suit a formal meeting.
“Useful feedback is just ‘good’ or ‘bad’.”
Name the feature and explain how it helps or what could change: “The labels are clear; could we put each one beside its object?”
activity: With a partner, plan a display of three paper models. Decide together how to take turns. Start the topic, invite a contribution, restate one idea, add a related suggestion, ask a relevant question and give one specific piece of feedback. Negotiate a change from arranging the models to choosing the title. Finish by checking what each person will do. Use the complete display cards in More examples for another short round.
adjust: Starter: an adult models one exchange about a different display; choose a useful question and complete one turn with a cue. Core: take part in the whole exchange and explain how one response helped. Stretch: use the same ideas in a chaired class meeting and explain which convention or wording you changed.
safety: Use speech, sign, AAC, writing or an agreed combination. Note prompting or modelling; a written choice supports understanding but does not demonstrate a real exchange. Do not require eye contact, a particular accent or immediate speech. Cultural learning uses named sources and checked host guidance.
tricky: 1. Can I disagree and still cooperate?
Yes. Explain the concern, connect it to the task and give others space to respond. Cooperation does not require everyone to hold the same view.
2. Can the same polite question suit a friend and a visitor?
Yes. Relationship, role, purpose and shared conventions matter. There is no need to force a different phrase when the same words work clearly.
3. Does one host’s speaking rule apply everywhere?
No. It tells you what to do in that supplied setting. Ask the actual hosts and use community-approved guidance for real events.
faq: How can I check that the group understands?
Ask someone to explain the next step or what they will do, then clarify any difference. “Does everyone understand?” alone may not reveal a misunderstanding.
What is the difference between a Welcome and an Acknowledgement?

A Welcome to Country has a specific Traditional Owner permission and delivery role. Anyone can offer an Acknowledgement of Country respectfully. Consult hosts and local representatives about the actual occasion.
modelCaption: A cooperative response connects to the contribution before it

title: Choose how strongly to express a view or feeling
intro: I can explain how words change a message’s certainty, requirement, judgement or emotion, and choose words that fit the context.
exampleTitle: A requirement and a possibility do different jobs
example: A class rule says, “You must wear shoes in the workshop.” Here, must states a requirement. A weather prediction says, “It might rain at lunchtime.” Here, might expresses a possibility. “You might wear shoes in the workshop” would weaken the rule into a possibility or suggestion, so it would not communicate the same requirement. Read the whole situation before explaining how forceful a word is.
steps: 1. Read modal verbs in context

Modal verbs such as must, might and could help express requirements, possibilities and other meanings. Ask what the speaker is doing: requiring an action, suggesting it or predicting what may happen. Compare versions of the same message in a stated context. There is no single strength ladder that explains every use of every modal.

Model A, a rule: “You must put the lid on the paint pot” makes the action required; “You could put the lid on the paint pot” offers it as a possibility or suggestion. Model B, a prediction: “The new lid might stop the paint drying out” leaves uncertainty; “The new lid will stop the paint drying out” presents the result more confidently. In “You must be tired after that long walk”, must expresses a strong conclusion, not an order to become tired.

The teacher is offering a choice of drawing materials, not making a rule: “You ___ use a pencil.” Choose could or must and explain. Then compare “The parcel might arrive today” with “The parcel will arrive today” as predictions.

Could suits the offered choice; must would make using a pencil sound required. Might presents arrival as possible, while will presents it more confidently. These are claims made by the speaker, not proof that the parcel will arrive. Context determines the intended meaning.
2. Notice how a narrator evaluates a character

An evaluation is a judgement or impression. Nouns can label a character, verbs can present how an action is done, and adverbs can add an attitude or degree. Compare exact words and explain the impression they invite. A changed word may add or change meaning, so it is not always a fact-preserving replacement.

Model A: “The visitor asked for another turn” presents a request; “The visitor demanded another turn” presents a more forceful insistence. Model B: “The guide patiently explained the route” suggests willingness to help; “The guide impatiently explained the route” suggests irritation. Calling a fictional character “a helper” rather than “a nuisance” also expresses approval rather than disapproval. Those noun labels are the narrator’s evaluations; they are not fair fixed labels for real people.

Compare these complete fictional versions: A “The captain calmly told the crew to wait.” B “The captain angrily ordered the crew to wait.” Which verb and adverb choices create the different impression? Give a more neutral version without claiming the captain’s feeling.

Told versus ordered changes the force of the instruction; calmly versus angrily changes the suggested attitude or emotion. A neutral version is “The captain told the crew to wait.” It removes the stated feeling. Another clear neutral reporting verb may work. Explain the changed meaning rather than say that one version is always better.
3. Choose emotion and judgement words with evidence

Words such as pleased, delighted, worried and terrified express different kinds or degrees of feeling. A judgement such as thoughtful or inventive evaluates a character or event. Use the text’s actions and words to support your choice. More forceful language is useful only when it suits the meaning and purpose.

Story A: “Tess found a missing library card. She took it straight to the desk so its owner could collect it.” “Tess was thoughtful” is a supported approving judgement because she considered the owner’s need. Story B: “A fox made a hidden trap to take all the other animals’ picnic food.” “The fox was sneaky” is supported by the secret, unfair plan. These judgements evaluate actions; neither word simply names an emotion. For feelings, “I am pleased with my drawing” can express mild satisfaction, while “I am delighted with my drawing” expresses stronger pleasure in this comparison.

Read this complete story: “Rae’s first paper tower fell. Rae changed the base and tried again. The second tower stood, and Rae smiled.” Choose persistent, careless or unkind as a supported judgement of Rae’s actions and explain. Then change “Rae felt pleased” to express stronger pleasure without changing it into fear.

Persistent fits because Rae kept trying and changed the design after a failure. The story does not support careless or unkind. “Rae felt delighted” is one stronger-pleasure version. Accept another suitable word with an explanation; smiling alone does not prove an exact hidden emotion. Distinguish your proposed wording from what the story directly states.
mistakes: “Must always gives an order.”
In “Visitors must sign in” it expresses a requirement. In “You must be tired” it expresses a strong conclusion. Read the whole situation.
“Every stronger word improves a text.”
A strong word can overstate a feeling, claim or instruction. Choose the force you actually mean.
“Asked and demanded mean exactly the same thing.”
Both can involve wanting something, but demanded adds forceful insistence. Substitution can change the character’s behaviour and the reader’s impression.
activity: Use the three complete revision cards in More examples. Make a suggestion less compulsory, change how a fictional narrator evaluates an action, and express a stronger feeling of pleasure. Explain the effect of each change using its actual context. Then write your own brief rule and uncertain prediction, and tell a partner how they differ.
adjust: Starter: choose between two words after an adult reads the complete context and explains an unfamiliar word. Core: make the three changes and explain the effect. Stretch: give two different context-appropriate versions of one message and explain why the more forceful one is useful in one situation but excessive in another.
safety: Discuss fictional actions and viewpoints without labelling classmates. Learners may explain orally, in writing or with communication support. Record support; choosing a word with a prompt is different from independently explaining its effect.
tricky: 1. Is “must not” the same as “do not have to”?
No. “You must not draw on the cover” forbids it. “You do not have to draw on the cover” says it is not required; that wording does not by itself forbid it.
2. Can one action have different evaluations?
Yes. A narrator might describe a firm request as helpful leadership or as bossy behaviour. Check the actual wording, evidence and viewpoint rather than treating an evaluation as a neutral fact.
3. Does an emotion word tell us how certain a prediction is?
Not by itself. Delighted describes pleasure. Might in “It might happen” expresses possibility. They change different parts of meaning.
faq: What is a modal verb?
It is a helping verb such as must, might, could or will that contributes meanings including requirement or possibility. Explain its job in the actual sentence.
Can two readers choose different judgement words?
Yes, if each meaning is accurate and supported by the text. An unsupported extreme judgement needs more evidence or a more suitable word.
modelCaption: Read the situation, identify the word choice, explain the changed meaning

title: Explain how a text’s organisation serves its purpose
intro: I can compare complete texts from different subjects and explain how their order, sections and word choices help do their jobs.
exampleTitle: The same topic can be organised for different jobs
example: Information: “Our class book box holds picture books and short chapter books. It stands beside the reading mat.” Request: “Please keep our class book box tidy. First, tidy books are easier to find. Second, returning each book helps the next reader. Let’s put books back after reading.” Both concern a book box. The information text groups facts to tell us about it. The request states a view, gives two reasons and ends with a call to act. Topic alone does not tell us purpose.
steps: 1. Compare a factual recount and an autobiography

A factual recount tells what happened on a particular occasion, usually placing events in time order. An autobiography is someone’s account of their own life or experiences. It commonly uses I or my, but I alone does not prove a text is autobiographical: fictional narrators use it too. Check who wrote it and whose experience is being recounted.

Prepared factual recount, written by the class reporter from the class record: “On Tuesday, Class 3 visited the school display. First, the class examined the paper models. Next, the guide explained how the labels were made. Finally, the class returned to its room.” Fictional model of an autobiographical account, written in the voice of the invented character Eli about Eli’s own life: “I moved to this town when I was six. At first, I did not know anyone at school. Later, I joined the drawing club and made a friend. Now I enjoy showing new children around.” The recount records one class event with past-tense actions and time links. Eli’s model selects personal experiences and ends by reflecting on the present.

Text A, written by a reporter: “On Friday, the team set up a paper display. First, they arranged the models. Then they added labels. They finished before lunch.” Text B, a fictional autobiographical model written in invented character Lani’s voice: “I learned to make models with my uncle when I was seven. At first, my towers fell. After many tries, I could build a tall one. I still enjoy designing new towers.” Explain one shared feature and one difference that helps each text’s purpose.

Both place past experiences in a useful time order. A recounts a particular team event and uses they. B presents Lani’s own selected experience through I/my and includes an ongoing personal reflection. Accept another accurate text-based comparison. A real autobiography is written by the person whose life it describes; the labelled classroom model is fictional.
2. Compare a report and a sequential explanation

An information report groups facts about a subject, often under headings. A sequential explanation shows how or why something happens through connected stages. Read all supplied facts: first/next links are useful, but an explanation also makes a process or connection clear. These choices help a reader find facts or follow how a result occurs.

Design report, “Our paper bridge”: “Materials: The bridge has a folded paper deck and two cardboard supports. Size: The deck is 20 centimetres long. Use: The model spans the gap between two trays.” Design explanation, “How the bridge holds the toy”: “First, the toy rests on the paper deck. The deck presses on the supports underneath it. The supports stand on the table, so they hold up the deck and toy.” The report groups material, size and use facts. The explanation follows the support relationship to explain how this prepared model holds the toy. It is a model-specific description, not a claim that every paper bridge supports every toy.

Report: “Class sorting boxes. Materials: Both boxes are cardboard. Labels: One box says Paper and the other says Card.” Explanation: “How we sort a card. First, we read its material label. If the label says card, we put it in the Card box. That keeps card together in this class sorting system.” Which text helps you find what the boxes are made of? Which helps you follow how a labelled card is sorted? Explain using organisation and words.

The report’s Materials section gives the cardboard fact directly. The explanation gives ordered actions and an if connection that explains the route to the Card box. It explains this supplied sorting system; no outside recycling rules are needed. Merely spotting the word first is less complete than explaining what the sequence does.
3. Compare a narrative, verse and a literary response

A narrative can introduce characters and a setting, develop a problem and show what follows. Verse poetry uses lines and may use sound, rhythm or imagery; it does not have to rhyme. A personal literary response gives a reader’s view of a supplied text and reasons grounded in it. These are useful patterns rather than rules every literary work must follow.

Narrative, “The runaway hat”: “In the playground, Nia’s paper hat blew over the bench. Nia chased it, but it caught in a bush. Omar held the branch still while Nia lifted the hat free. Nia thanked Omar and tucked the hat into her bag.” Verse, “Paper hat”: “Paper hat, a little sail, / skips along a windy trail. / Catch it gently, hold it tight; / fold the wind away tonight.” Personal response to “The runaway hat”: “I enjoyed the ending because Omar helps Nia solve the problem. Holding the branch is a small action that makes their teamwork clear.” The story links a problem and solution; the verse uses four lines, rhyme and an imagined sail; the response names a judgement and supports it with the actual story.

Narrative, “The lost label”: “Ari could not find the label for a model boat. Bea checked under the display cloth and found it. Together they put the label beside the boat before the visitors arrived.” Verse, “Little label”: “Small paper sign, / beside the boat: / you tell its name / without a voice.” Which text uses lines and an imagined voice to focus attention on the label? Give a personal response to the narrative with a reason from its events.

The verse uses four lines and imagines the sign communicating without a voice; it does not rhyme, which is allowed. A possible response is “I liked the teamwork because Bea finds the label and both children put it in place.” Other preferences, including a reasoned dislike, are valid when grounded in an actual event. A retelling alone does not express and support a personal judgement.
4. Follow the stages of a simple argument

A simple argument aims to persuade a reader to accept a view or act. In this model, an introduction states the view, two arguments give relevant reasons, and a conclusion returns to the view. A fact that merely mentions the topic does not necessarily support the view. Compare a complete argument with information about the same subject.

Argument: “Our class should keep a paper-scrap tray. First, usable scraps would be easy to find for small drawings. Second, keeping them in one place would help us reuse paper. For these reasons, let’s put a scrap tray beside the art shelf.” Introduction: the first sentence states the proposal. Argument one: finding usable scraps. Argument two: reusing paper. Conclusion: the last sentence returns to the proposal and asks for action. Information comparison: “The paper tray is beside the art shelf. It is shallow and blue. It holds pieces of drawing paper.” That comparison describes the tray without asking the reader to support it.

Read this whole argument: “We should put names on our model labels. First, visitors could see who made each model. Second, a visitor with a question could find its maker. Let’s add our first names before the display opens.” Identify the introduction, both reasons and conclusion. Explain why “The labels are rectangular” would not be a useful replacement for the second reason.

The introduction proposes names; reason one links names to identifying makers; reason two links names to asking the maker questions; the final sentence asks for action. Rectangular describes shape but does not explain why names should be added. It is related to labels without supporting the stated proposal. For this fictional class task, use invented names rather than sharing personal details online.
mistakes: “A text’s topic tells me its purpose.”
Two texts about a tray can describe it or persuade people to use it. Examine what the writer asks the reader to know, imagine, feel or do.
“One signal word proves the text type.”
Read the whole text and explain how its organisation and language work together. First can appear in a recount, explanation or argument.
“Every poem rhymes and every story has the same shape.”
Poems can use unrhymed lines. Stories can arrange events in different ways. Describe the choices in the actual text.
activityTitle: Sort texts by the job they do
activity: Read the complete comparison cards in More examples, one pair at a time. For each text, name its main purpose, point to an organisation choice and one language clue, then explain how they help the reader. Finish by comparing the information card and argument about the same object. Use the texts themselves instead of guessing from a label alone.
adjust: Starter: an adult reads one contrasting pair; choose between two purposes and point to a supporting phrase. Core: compare both structure and language for the supplied pairs. Stretch: change an informative model into a short persuasive request with an introduction, two relevant reasons and a conclusion; explain the changes.
safety: All classroom texts are supplied original models; the autobiographical voices are explicitly fictional. Read a pair in a short session and allow oral explanation or a scribe. Record support and use a fresh card for independent evidence.
tricky: 1. Does I always mean a real autobiography?
No. A fictional narrator can say I. Check whether the writer is recounting their own actual life; these classroom autobiographical models are labelled fictional.
2. Is every ordered text an explanation?
No. A recount orders what happened, a procedure tells someone what to do, and a sequential explanation shows how or why a process happens. Explain the job of the sequence in the actual text.
3. Must I agree with a model response to a story?
No. Give your own view and a relevant reason grounded in the supplied story. Different supported responses can be valid.
faq: What should I say after naming a structure?
Point to the actual feature and explain its use: “Materials groups the making facts, so I can find what the model is made from.”
Can texts mix purposes or structures?
Yes. These short models make their main purposes clear for learning. In a longer text, describe the feature and its local job rather than force every part into one label.
modelCaption: Compare purpose, organisation and language using the whole text

title: Use paragraphs to group and develop ideas
intro: I can explain how paragraphs group related information, improve their order and compare informative and narrative paragraph choices.
exampleTitle: An opening gives the details a shared focus
example: “Our model garden has a clear layout. A wide path runs between the beds. Labels name the plants beside each bed. A sign by the gate shows the route.” The first sentence introduces the layout; the other sentences develop it with a path, labels and a route sign. “The sign is by the gate” would introduce only one narrow detail. A useful topic sentence prepares us for the whole paragraph.
steps: 1. Group information and develop the topic

A paragraph groups related information. In an informative text, a topic sentence often comes first and predicts the focus. Supporting sentences explain, describe or give examples of that focus. Read all the details before deciding whether an opening is too narrow, too broad or suitable.

Model A: “Our class display is easy to explore. Each model has a clear label. A wide gap lets visitors move between tables. Arrows show the route.” All details explain ease of exploring. Model B: “Our model box protects the contents. Thick sides surround the models. Folded paper separates them. A lid keeps loose pieces inside.” All details explain protection. The paragraphs develop different topics even though both concern models.

Details: “Two handles make the basket easy to lift. A wide opening lets us reach the books. A flat base keeps it steady.” Choose an opening: A “Our book basket is useful.” B “Our basket has two handles.” C “All baskets are wonderful.” Explain using all three details.

A is best supported: the handles, opening and base each explain a useful feature of this basket. B covers only the handles. C claims something about every basket that these details do not show. Other accurate openings with a similar whole-paragraph focus are valid.
2. Order and repair paragraphs for the reader

Choose which details belong together, then arrange them so readers can follow references and explanations. Introduce a thing before using it or its when needed for clarity. Move an unrelated detail to a suitable paragraph instead of deleting useful information without a reason. A paragraph break should mark an idea or stage, not simply a fixed number of sentences.

Draft: “The class display has three models. They stand on a low table. Our labels use large writing. Each label names a model. It is wide enough for visitors to see all three.” The final it is unclear. Repair: “The class display has three models. They stand on a low table. The table is wide enough for visitors to see all three.” New paragraph: “Our labels use large writing. Each label names a model.” The repair groups arrangement details separately from label details and names the table. Contrast: placing every sentence in a new paragraph would hide these useful groups.

Arrange these sentences into two paragraphs and explain the groups: A “Each pot has a plant name beside it.” B “Our pots have clear labels.” C “The watering can is kept by the door.” D “Our watering tools are easy to find.” E “A jug stands beside the can.” F “The names help us identify the plants.”

One clear arrangement is B, A, F for the label paragraph, then D, C, E for the tools paragraph. The first sentence in each group introduces its topic; the details develop it. C before E identifies the can before the reference the can. Reversing the two whole paragraphs may also work; explain a useful order rather than insist on one unsupported order for independent topics.
3. Notice narrative paragraph choices

Narrative paragraphs can mark a new event, time, place, speaker or moment of emphasis. They vary in length and do not always begin with a topic sentence that announces the idea. Look at the actual break and explain what changes there. A one-sentence paragraph can be purposeful; length alone does not decide quality.

Narrative model: “At the display table, Isla searched for her paper bird. She looked behind the box and under the cloth.” New paragraph: “A soft rustle came from the doorway.” New paragraph: “Isla hurried over. Her paper bird was caught beside the door. She lifted it carefully and carried it back.” The short middle paragraph gives the sound its own moment, before the action shifts to the doorway. Contrast the informative model “Our box protects the models. Thick sides surround them.” Its opening predicts supporting information; the narrative does not follow that same formula.

Read these narrative paragraphs: “At lunchtime, Ravi left his model on the classroom shelf. He planned to add its label later.” New paragraph: “After lunch, the shelf was empty.” New paragraph: “Ravi asked the teacher. She had moved the model to the display table.” Explain what changes at the first break and why the short middle paragraph may be useful.

The first break marks a time change from lunchtime to after lunch and a new problem. The short middle paragraph puts attention on the missing model; the next paragraph gives the search and explanation. It does not need an informative opening such as “This paragraph is about a missing model.” Other reasonable effect explanations are valid when linked to the actual break.
mistakes: “Every paragraph must have three sentences.”
Paragraph length depends on purpose and the amount of related information. Narrative paragraphs can be very short.
“A topic sentence repeats one detail.”
It should prepare the reader for the paragraph’s whole focus. Check it against all supporting details.
“A new line after every sentence creates good paragraphs.”
Group related sentences and use breaks for meaningful changes. Blank lines help show the groups but cannot organise unrelated ideas for you.
activityTitle: Build two paragraphs and explain one break
activity: Use the complete sorting and narrative cards in More examples. Group the information sentences into two focused paragraphs, choose an opening for each and read them back. Repair any unclear reference. Then read the supplied short narrative and explain one paragraph break using its time, event or emphasis change.
adjust: Starter: an adult reads and displays sentence cards; sort two clear topics, then choose an opening from two options. Core: arrange and explain two paragraphs and one narrative break. Stretch: offer another workable narrative break or paragraph order, preserving meaning, and explain the effect on the reader.
safety: Use cut-up copies or point to sentence letters without cutting. Allow dictation or oral explanation and note the support. Judge grouping and reasoning rather than handwriting speed or a fixed paragraph length.
tricky: 1. Does every narrative paragraph begin with a topic sentence?
No. A narrative may begin with a sound, action or speech. Its paragraph choices can organise events or create emphasis without announcing a main idea.
2. Must independent information paragraphs always go in one order?
No. Sometimes either order is useful. Follow any stated purpose or reference links, and explain your choice.
3. Should I delete an unrelated but useful sentence?
It may fit a different paragraph. Move it to the matching group when that preserves useful information and improves the organisation.
faq: What makes a supporting detail useful?
It develops the paragraph’s focus by explaining, describing, giving a reason or offering an example.
How do I check a paragraph repair?
Read each paragraph as a group. Name its focus, check every sentence belongs and make sure references and sequence remain clear.
modelCaption: One paragraph develops one connected focus or stage

title: Use headings and links to find your way through texts
intro: I can explain how print and digital layout features guide readers, follow useful navigation words and check the information I find.
exampleTitle: A specific label helps you choose a useful route
example: In the prepared class garden guide, the broad heading “Visiting” groups two subheadings: “Opening times” and “Where to enter”. To find when the garden opens, choose “Opening times” and read its information: “Our model garden opens after the morning bell.” The broad heading suggests a route; the specific subheading names the information you need. A heading is a guide, so check the actual text after choosing it.
steps: 1. Read headings, subheadings and chapter titles

A heading names a topic or section. A subheading names a smaller part within it. Their size and position can show the relationship. A narrative chapter title may hint at an event or make us curious without giving the whole event away. In print, use a contents page and page number when supplied, then check the actual chapter or section.

Print guide model: title “Class garden guide”; heading “Visiting”; subheadings “Opening times” and “Where to enter”. “Opening times” contains “Our model garden opens after the morning bell.” “Where to enter” contains “Use the gate beside the shed.” Contrast a narrative contents card: Chapter 1 “The empty shelf”, page 3; Chapter 2 “A rustle by the door”, page 7. Chapter 2 begins, “Mina heard paper rustling by the door. Her missing paper bird was caught beside it.” The chapter title hints at a sound; the actual text explains its source.

A print model has the heading “Making our display”, with subheadings “Materials” and “Labels”. Under Materials it says, “We used paper and card.” Under Labels it says, “Write the model’s name on each label.” Which is the most specific subheading for finding what the models are made from? Then explain what a chapter called “The hidden box” might make you expect and what you still need to check.

Materials is the most specific route; its text supplies paper and card. “The hidden box” may suggest that a box is concealed or discovered, but the title does not prove who hid it or what is inside. Read the actual chapter before claiming those details. Different reasonable predictions are valid when clearly labelled as predictions.
2. Follow meaningful hyperlink words

A hyperlink connects to a destination. Its words should help predict what will be found there. Read the link text, follow it and check the destination heading and content. A menu groups routes; words such as return or next describe movement within a particular prepared text. The working model below uses real links on this page.

In the working garden model, “Opening times” leads to a section with that heading and the morning-bell information. “Where to enter” leads to a different section with the shed-gate information. Each destination has a “Return to garden menu” link that leads back to the menu. Contrast an unclear label “More”: by itself it does not say which garden information is behind it. Meaningful link words help a reader choose a route, but the destination still needs checking.

Use the working garden links in this section. Find which gate to use, then return to the menu. Name the link you followed and the heading and information that confirmed the destination. Explain why “Where to enter” is more useful here than “More”.

Follow Where to enter; the matching destination heading and “Use the gate beside the shed” confirm the route. Return to garden menu brings you back to the menu. The specific link predicts entry information, while More alone leaves its topic unclear. Pointing to printed words shows a route choice; actually following the native link demonstrates this navigation task.
3. Compare routes and check what you found

Print and digital texts can share useful headings while offering different ways to reach them. A printed page reference guides you to a page; a digital link can move directly to a destination. Choose a route for the information need, then verify the heading and relevant sentence. If the information does not match, return and choose another route rather than guessing.

Print comparison: the prepared guide’s contents lists “Visiting”, page 4; on page 4, “Opening times” and “Where to enter” divide the information. Digital comparison: the prepared garden menu links directly to those two sections. Both can answer an entry question. A page number tells where to look in the model book; hyperlink words tell what the digital destination concerns. Neither replaces reading the information itself.

Use the print and digital tool-storage cards in this section. Find where the trowels belong by each route. Explain one difference between the routes and quote or restate the sentence that confirms the same answer.

In the print model, choose Tool storage in the contents, go to page 6 and read the Trowels subheading. In the digital model, follow Trowel storage to that named section. Both state that trowels belong on the lower shelf. The print page reference and digital link are different routes to the same supplied information. Check both the destination and the relevant sentence.
mistakes: “The largest heading must give the exact answer.”
A large heading often names a broad topic. A subheading may give the more specific route; read its text to check.
“A chapter title tells me every event.”
It can hint or create curiosity. Predictions need checking against the chapter.
“A useful-looking link proves the destination is right.”
Follow the link and check the destination heading and information. Clear words help you predict; the text confirms.
activityTitle: Find it in print and on the model page
activity: Use the complete print and working digital cards in More examples. Find an opening time, the entry gate and the place for trowels. For each search, name the feature you used and the sentence that confirms the answer. Compare a print page route with a digital link route. Then suggest a more informative label for a vague “More” link to tool-storage information.
adjust: Starter: an adult reads two labelled routes; choose the useful one and find the confirming sentence together. Core: follow the print and actual digital routes and explain their purposes. Stretch: improve a vague heading or link label while preserving its destination, and explain why a reader could choose the route more easily.
safety: These are small prepared models with local page anchors; no account or personal information is needed. Adults may support device access. Distinguish choosing a route on paper from observing actual digital navigation; record the support used.
tricky: 1. Can a broad heading and a subheading both help?
Yes. Visiting can lead you to the right broad section; Opening times is the more specific label for when visits are possible. State whether you are naming a route or the most specific destination.
2. Does “Next” always mean the same place?
It means the next destination in that particular text or sequence. Check where it leads; the word alone does not name a universal page.
3. Can I infer what is in “The hidden box” from the title alone?
You can make a prediction about a hidden box, but the title cannot establish its contents. Read the actual chapter to check.
faq: What is a hyperlink?
It is a link to another location, here a real named section within the prepared page. Its visible words should help you predict the destination.
Why compare print and digital versions?
Both organise information for readers. Comparing them shows how headings, page references, menus and links provide routes, and why readers still need to check what they find.
modelCaption: Choose a route, reach the destination, check the information

title: Find clauses and match subjects with verbs
intro: I can find the subject and verb in a clause and make them agree in standard written English.
example: Read the whole sentence: “While the puppy slept, the kittens played beside the basket.” Slept links to the puppy; played links to the kittens. There are two clauses. “While the puppy slept” has a subject and verb, but it needs the rest of the sentence here. A clause is usually built around a subject and a verb; it does not always stand alone as a sentence.
steps: 1. Find the verb and its subject

Look for the verb or whole verb group. Ask who or what that verb tells us about. Include the words that belong with the subject. A subject can name someone doing something, or something being described.

In “The little gate is open”, the subject is “The little gate” and the verb is “is”. Is relates the gate to a description. In “While the puppy slept, the kittens played beside the basket”, the pairs are the puppy / slept and the kittens / played.
Find the two subject–verb pairs in “While the rain fell, the children were painting indoors.”

The rain / fell is one pair; the children / were painting is the other. Keep were with painting as the whole verb group. The while clause belongs with the rest of this sentence; it is not a complete sentence by itself here.
2. Match one or more than one

In ordinary present-tense examples with he, she, it or one named person or thing, many verbs end in -s: the duck swims. With a plural noun subject, use the matching plural form: the ducks swim. Find the main naming word in a longer subject rather than matching the nearest noun.

“The box of pencils sits on the shelf.” Box is one thing, so sits matches it. “The pencils in the box sit on the shelf.” Pencils is plural, so sit matches it. “Mina and Jo carry the box” has two people joined by and, so carry is the matching form.
Choose the form in each sentence: “The bag of shells rest/rests here.” “Sam and Lee carry/carries it.” Explain which words helped.

Use rests because the subject names one bag. Use carry because Sam and Lee names two people. Of shells does not turn the one bag into a plural subject. The -s pattern is for these present-tense verbs, not a rule for every verb and tense.
3. Check special forms and repair

Read the whole clause, find the subject, and check its verb form. Be and have have special forms: I am, she is, they are; she has, they have. In the past, I/he/she/it was and we/you/they were are useful standard written patterns.

Draft: “The twins is ready. Their sister have a bag.” Revised: “The twins are ready. Their sister has a bag.” Twins is plural; sister is singular. These are agreement repairs. The clauses already contained verbs, even though their forms needed changing.
Repair “We was by the gate. The small dog have a lead.” Keep the first event in the past and the second description in the present.

Write “We were by the gate. The small dog has a lead.” Were agrees with we in this past-time clause; has agrees with the singular dog in the present-time description. Different times are allowed when that is the intended meaning.
mistakes: “Every clause is a complete sentence.”
A clause can depend on nearby words: “While the puppy slept” needs the rest of the model sentence.
“Match the verb to the closest noun.”
Find the subject’s main naming word: the bag of shells rests; the shells in the bag rest.
“All singular verbs end in -s.”
Check the particular verb and pronoun. I swim, you swim and she swims are standard present forms; be has special forms.
activity: Use the complete clause cards in More examples. Read each sentence, mark the whole subject and verb group, and repair any agreement error. Then join the two supplied clauses with while and explain why the while part needs its partner. Say which naming word controls each repair.
adjust: Starter: use the first two cards with an adult and mark subject and verb in two different ways. Core: complete all cards and explain the agreement repairs. Stretch: expand a subject with of or in, then explain why that added noun does not control the verb.
safety: An adult may read the sentences aloud. Compare the standard written forms being taught without judging a learner’s home dialect or language. Note any modelling used.
tricky: 1. Is “is” a verb in “The gate is open”?
Yes. It relates the gate to its description; a verb need not describe an action.
2. Does every plural subject end in -s?
No. Children is plural. Context also tells us whether sheep names one or more than one.
3. Can a command have a subject we cannot see?
Yes. In “Close the gate”, you is understood. Most examples here show the subject explicitly, which makes the partnership easier to inspect.
faq: Do I circle only the action word?
Find the whole verb group when there is more than one word: were painting, not painting alone.
Why learn agreement?
Matching forms helps readers follow standard written sentences. First identify who or what the clause is about, then check the form.
modelCaption: Two clauses in one complete sentence
modelCards: the kittens / played beside the basket
Keep its verb or verb group

title: Choose verbs for different kinds of meaning
intro: I can explain how verbs tell about doing, saying, thinking, feeling and relating.
exampleTitle: Verbs let us see events and know thoughts
example: Read this original story: “Mila lifted the lid. ‘It is empty,’ she whispered. She remembered the missing seeds and loved the idea of finding them. The box had a loose hinge.” Lifted tells an action; whispered tells how words were spoken; remembered tells thinking; loved tells feeling. Is relates it to empty, and had relates the box to something it possessed. The verbs give different kinds of information.
steps: 1. Follow doing and saying in a story
Doing verbs tell what happens or what a character does. Saying verbs tell that someone communicates words. Choose a precise verb and explain what it contributes in this clause.

In the story, lifted shows Mila’s action with the lid. Whispered is a saying verb: it tells us she spoke quietly. Compare “Mila said, ‘It is empty’” with “Mila shouted, ‘It is empty’”. The words stay the same, but shouted suggests a louder delivery; the reason for it still needs context.
In “Jo pushed the gate. ‘Come in,’ Jo called”, find a doing verb and a saying verb. What does each tell us?
Pushed tells what Jo did to the gate. Called tells us Jo spoke the invitation, with a voice intended to reach someone. Do not decide Jo is angry from called alone; context matters.
2. Notice thinking and feeling
Some verbs let the reader know a character’s thoughts or feelings, even when these cannot be seen directly. Read the surrounding words to decide the kind of meaning being expressed.

“Ari remembered the old path” tells a thought from memory. “Ari disliked the loud bell” tells a feeling about it. These are sensing meanings. Neither has to name a visible movement. A face may give a clue, but these verbs tell the reader directly about the inner experience.
In “Nia believed the story. She loved its friendly dragon”, which verb tells thinking and which tells feeling?

Believed tells what Nia thought was true. Loved tells her feeling about the dragon. The sentence context makes the meanings clear. Some verbs can be discussed in more than one way in other contexts; explain the meaning here.
3. Use relating verbs to describe and define
Relating verbs connect a subject with what it is, what it is like or what it has. They are useful in descriptions and definitions. Look at the whole clause: is and has can also help other verbs.

“A triangle is a shape with three straight sides.” Is relates triangle to a definition. “The model bird has a long beak.” Has relates the model bird to a feature. Compare “The bird is hopping”: is helps hopping; the whole group describes doing.
In “The toy boats are small. Each boat has a sail. The boats are moving”, identify the relating verbs and the whole doing verb group.

Are in “are small” relates the boats to their size. Has relates each boat to a sail. Are moving is the whole group telling an action; are is helping moving there. Classify the meaning of the clause, not a word on its own.
mistakes: “A verb always means an action I can act out.”
Thinking, feeling and relating verbs also carry meaning: remembered, loved and is are verbs in the model.
“Has is always a relating verb.”
Has relates possession in “She has a bag”. In “She has packed”, it helps packed. Read the whole group.
“A louder saying verb proves anger.”
A character might shout to be heard over a crowd. Use the whole story before deciding the feeling.
activityTitle: Tell a small story with five meanings
activity: Use the complete story and verb cards in More examples. Sort each highlighted verb by its meaning in that clause, then explain the information it gives. Write your own three or four connected sentences about finding a lost pencil. Include doing, saying, thinking, feeling and relating meanings; more than one can appear in a sentence.
adjust: Starter: compare a doing clause with a relating clause using the given cards. Core: explain all five meanings in the supplied story and use them in your own writing. Stretch: change one saying or doing verb and explain the new detail without inventing an unsupported feeling.
safety: Use invented characters and feelings; learners need not disclose personal experiences. An adult may read the text or scribe the learner’s own clauses.
tricky: 1. Can “is” be a complete verb?
Yes: “The box is empty” uses is to relate the box to a description. It does not need an action verb.
2. Are “think” and “thinking” always the whole verb group?
No. In “Jo was thinking”, keep was with thinking when naming the whole group.
3. Must one word always keep one process label?
No. Meaning depends on its use in a clause. Give a reason from this sentence; use a clearer example if a classification is uncertain.
faq: Why choose a precise verb?
It can add useful information: crept suggests a different movement from ran. Choose the one that matches your intended event.
What does relating mean?
It connects someone or something to an identity, description or possession, as in “The box is empty” and “It has a lid”.
modelCards: Relating: is empty / had a hinge

title: Use verb forms to show time clearly
intro: I can use verb forms and time clues to explain when events happen and keep a short text clear.
exampleTitle: The verb carries a time clue
example: Compare “Yesterday Nia walked to the gate”, “Nia is walking to the gate now” and “Tomorrow Nia will walk to the gate”. Walked shows past time, is walking shows an action happening now in this context, and will walk points to a future event here. Yesterday, now and tomorrow add time information; they do not replace the need for matching verb forms.
steps: 1. Read the whole verb group and context

Find the verb or whole group, then read the time words and surrounding sentences. Present forms can describe habits or facts as well as what happens now. A present form can also describe a future arrangement when the context makes that clear.

“Nia walks to school each day” describes a habit. “Nia is walking now” describes the current action. “It is Monday. Nia is arriving on Tuesday” uses is arriving with a future-time phrase. Look at both form and context rather than claiming that every present form means right now.
Explain the time in “Every morning Jo feeds the hens” and “Tomorrow Jo will feed the hens”. Name each whole verb group.

Feeds describes a repeated habit, supported by every morning. Will feed points to a future event, supported by tomorrow. Keep both words in will feed. The verb forms and time expressions work together.
2. Change regular and irregular forms

Many past forms use -ed, such as play → played. Other verbs change differently, such as catch → caught. Learn and check common forms instead of adding -ed to every word. When using will for a future event, use the base form after it.
“She catches the ball” becomes “She caught the ball” for the past event. “They jump” becomes “They jumped”. “She will catch the ball tomorrow” uses catch after will, without the present-tense -es.
Tell yesterday’s events: “Lee carries the tray. Lee takes a cup.” Then complete “Tomorrow Lee will ___ the tray” using carry.
Write “Lee carried the tray. Lee took a cup.” Carry changes to carried; take has the irregular past took. Write “Tomorrow Lee will carry the tray.” Use the base carry after will.
3. Keep a sequence clear, and change time for a reason

For events in one past recount, use matching past forms unless you mean to change time. A new time phrase can help the reader understand a deliberate change to a current fact or a future plan. Consistency means clear intended timing, not forcing every verb in a text into one tense.

Draft: “Yesterday we packed the seeds. We carry the box to the shed.” Revised: “Yesterday we packed the seeds. We carried the box to the shed.” Both are past events. “Yesterday we planted seeds. Today we water them” deliberately changes time and says so.

This draft tells two events from yesterday and one plan for tomorrow: “Yesterday Sam found a pot. He puts soil in it. Tomorrow he will plant a seed.” Repair the unclear verb and explain which change of time should stay.

Change puts to put: “Yesterday Sam found a pot. He put soil in it. Tomorrow he will plant a seed.” Found and put are the two past events; put looks the same as its base form. Keep will plant because tomorrow marks the intended future plan.
mistakes: “Yesterday makes any verb form past.”
Read the verb too. In standard written recounts, yesterday we walk needs walked for the intended completed past event.
“Every past verb ends in -ed.”
Common irregular forms include took, caught, went and put. Check the particular word.
“A text must never change tense.”
It may move from a past event to a current fact or future plan. Make the intended change clear.
activity: Use the complete time cards in More examples. Read the context, change the marked verbs to fit it, and explain the evidence for each form. Finish with a three-sentence garden message: one past event, one present habit and one future plan. Give enough time clues for a reader to follow the changes.
adjust: Starter: compare past and present cards with a supplied verb bank. Core: repair a short recount and explain one irregular form. Stretch: write a clear text that deliberately moves from a past event to a future plan, and explain why the shift belongs.
safety: An adult can read or scribe while the learner chooses and explains verb forms. Accept a clear oral explanation before written practice; record the support used.
tricky: 1. Does present always mean this very second?
No. “Birds have feathers” states a general fact; “Jo walks each morning” states a habit.
2. Is “will carries” right for tomorrow?
Use “will carry”. The base form follows will in this construction.
3. How can I know the time if a word does not change?
Use the whole clause and context. “Yesterday I put it here” describes the past even though put keeps the same form.
faq: What are time adverbials?
Words or groups that add time information, such as yesterday, now or in the morning. They work alongside verb forms.
Must I use will for every future event?
No. “We are going to plant tomorrow” and “We are planting tomorrow” can also express future plans in a clear context. Will plus a base verb is one useful pattern.
modelCaption: Read verb forms together with their time clues

title: Explain what a picture adds to words
intro: I can use visible details to explain how an image adds meaning, while separating evidence from a possible interpretation.
exampleTitle: The words name a meeting; the picture adds a relationship
example: The meeting illustration says “Jo met Kim.” Its image adds that the two figures stand near one another, turn towards each other and smile. Their hands reach towards the same box. These details can suggest a friendly shared activity. The words alone do not tell us this, and the image does not prove how long they have known each other. Describe what is visible before explaining what it may suggest.
steps: 1. Look at relationships between characters

Notice who faces whom, the space between figures, their depicted sizes, where they look, and their expressions and gestures. Use several details together. Looking up at a larger figure may suggest unequal power in a story, but size can also show age or distance from the viewer.

In the meeting model, closeness, faces turned towards each other, smiles and hands reaching towards one box support a possible cooperative relationship. In the gate model below, one figure is drawn larger, looks down and points; the other looks up. That arrangement may make the larger figure seem in charge. It does not prove that the figure is unkind.
Use the separate gate try illustration. What does the image add to “The two people waited”? Give two visible details and one cautious interpretation.

The figures are far apart and face away from each other, with their arms folded. These details may suggest distance or a disagreement in this scene. They could have other reasons for waiting that way; the image does not tell us the cause. Accept another plausible interpretation supported by the actual details.
2. Notice the relationship with the viewer

Gaze means the direction someone looks. A character looking towards the viewer can invite us into the scene. A close view makes a face prominent; a wide view can make the setting and space more noticeable. These choices can affect our response without proving one emotion.

The viewer model below pairs the words “Ari waited” with two images. The close face looks out towards us, which can invite attention to Ari. The wide view shows a small Ari turned away in a large empty space, which can suggest distance or loneliness. The written words stay the same.
Compare the two library try pictures below, both captioned “May chose a book”. Which view invites more attention to May’s expression? Which shows more of the space? Use visible evidence.

The close view makes May’s smiling face large and shows a gaze towards the viewer, inviting us to notice her response. The wide view makes May much smaller and shows the surrounding shelves and open floor. Learners may respond differently; judge the visible evidence and explanation, not a required feeling.
3. Separate words, visible facts and possibilities

First say what the words tell you. Next name information actually visible in the image. Then explain a possible meaning supported by those details. Say what remains unknown. A map or diagram can add useful information in the same way.

For the arrival picture below, the words say “We finally arrived.” The image adds mud marks on two children’s clothes and a map with a jagged tear. Those details may suggest a difficult journey, but do not tell us exactly what happened. The retained creek map adds the location of a bridge and a route that its sentence does not give.
For the arrival picture, sort these claims: “They arrived”; “Their clothes have mud marks”; “They fell into the creek”. Which comes from the words, which is visible and which is not established?

“They arrived” comes from the words. Mud marks are visible in the illustration. Falling into a creek is not established: neither words nor picture shows how the mud got there. A hard journey is a supported possibility, not a known backstory.
mistakes: “The picture is nice” explains its meaning.
Name the detail and its contribution: the figures face one another and share a box, which may suggest cooperation.
“A big character must be powerful or bad.”
Describe size alongside gaze, gesture and story context. A close figure can look bigger because of position.
“I can treat my guess as a fact.”
Separate what is stated, what is visible and what might be true. Explain the evidence for your interpretation.
activity: Use the actual meeting, gate and viewer illustrations in More examples. Choose one caption and draw a different image for it. Change two useful details, such as spacing and gaze. Explain what your picture adds and compare a possible interpretation with the original. Finish by naming something neither version establishes.
adjust: Starter: point to two visible details with an adult, using the supplied image descriptions if needed. Core: explain what the picture adds and support an inference with two details. Stretch: keep the words the same, change a visual choice and explain a different possible reader response.
safety: Accessible descriptions supply the depicted evidence without assigning a feeling. Discuss constructed fictional images; do not judge real people’s feelings, honesty or ability from eye contact, body position or size.
tricky: 1. Does facing away always mean disagreement?
No. People might be looking at something else. It is a possible story meaning when other details support it.
2. Does a close-up guarantee everyone feels involved?
No. It makes selected detail prominent. Explain what you notice and how it may invite attention in this context.
3. Can a useful image add information without showing faces?
Yes. The creek map adds a bridge location and walking route. A diagram can also show how parts connect.
faq: What counts as evidence?
A specific visible feature, such as the gap between figures, the direction of gaze, a smile, a labelled bridge or the route line.
Can two interpretations be reasonable?
Yes, if each fits the actual words and image. Accept supported possibilities and identify what the text does not establish.
modelCaption: Read the words, inspect the image, explain the added meaning

title: Grow precise vocabulary and check meaning in context
intro: I can use useful topic words, explain a word’s meaning in its sentence and build related words with meaningful parts.
exampleTitle: The same word can do different jobs
example: “The cup felt warm in my hands” describes temperature. “The story has a warm character who welcomes everyone” describes a friendly, kind person. Hands and cup help with the first meaning; welcomes everyone helps with the second. A word can have more than one meaning. Use its sentence, topic and nearby explanation to choose a meaning that fits.
steps: 1. Use precise length words

Technical words name ideas precisely in a topic. Millimetre and centimetre name metric units of length. A centimetre contains ten millimetres. Give a number and unit together when reporting a measured length; the unit tells what the number counts.

In this supplied measurement record, a paper strip is 8 centimetres long and 2 centimetres wide. A different thin strip is 6 millimetres wide. “The strip is 8 long” leaves out the unit. “The paper strip is 8 centimetres long” gives a clear measurement.
Use this supplied record: ribbon length 12 centimetres; ribbon width 5 millimetres. Write one sentence reporting both dimensions with precise words.

For example, “The ribbon is 12 centimetres long and 5 millimetres wide.” Retain the two numbers and their matching units. This is vocabulary practice using given measurements; you do not need to guess a real ribbon’s size.
2. Use the vocabulary of stories

A character is a person, animal or other figure in a story. Setting tells where and when the events happen. Plot is the connected events, including a problem and what happens about it. Use these terms to describe an actual text rather than only reciting definitions.

Original story: “At dusk in the school garden, a toy robot named Pip lost a wheel. A snail rolled it back. Pip fixed the wheel and went home.” Pip and the snail are characters; dusk in the school garden gives the setting. Losing, returning and fixing the wheel are connected plot events.
Read: “One rainy morning in a shed, a mouse named Fen found a locked box. Fen fetched a key and opened it.” Name a character, the setting and two connected plot events.

Fen is a character. One rainy morning in a shed gives time and place. Finding the locked box, fetching a key and opening it form the plot sequence; accept any two of those connected events. The shed alone is a place, not the plot.
3. Choose a meaning using context clues

Read the whole sentence and nearby words. Try a possible meaning in place of the word and check whether it fits. A familiar technical word can have an everyday meaning too; do not lock one word to only one meaning.

“The class will plot the plant heights on a graph” uses plot to mean mark or show data. “The story’s plot includes a lost wheel” uses plot for connected story events. Graph and heights support the first sense; story and events support the second.
Explain light in “This empty box is light enough to lift” and “The lamp gives us light to read by”. Give a clue for each meaning.

In the first sentence, light means not heavy; empty box and lift support that sense. In the second, light means illumination; lamp and read by support it. Substituting each explanation should keep the intended message.
4. Build a word family, then check the sentence

A prefix comes before a base, and a suffix comes after it. These parts can change meaning or how a word works. Re- can mean again; un- can mean not; -ful can mean having a quality; -ly can help describe how something is done. Only use combinations that are real words and fit the context.

“Jo reread the note” uses re- + read: Jo read it again. “The unhelpful clue confused us” uses un- + help + -ful: the clue did not help. “Jo spoke differently” uses different + -ly to describe how Jo spoke. Related words can change form: “We noticed a difference” names what was different.
Complete the two messages using real related words: “The first label was unclear, so I will ___ it” (write again). “Jo gave a ___ answer that helped us” (help + a suffix). Explain the added meaning.

Use rewrite for write again, and helpful for an answer that helps. Re- adds again; -ful builds the describing word helpful. Read the completed sentences to check the meanings. Do not add an affix to every word just because its meaning seems useful.
mistakes: “A technical word needs no explanation.”
Introduce its meaning and use it accurately in a sentence. A number such as 12 needs its measurement unit.
“One word has only one meaning.”
Plot can name story events or mark data. Use the topic and surrounding words to choose.
“I can attach any prefix to any word.”
Word parts give clues, but check that the result is a real word with the intended meaning in this sentence.
activityTitle: Make a useful four-part word notebook
activity: Use the complete vocabulary cards in More examples. Write a precise measurement sentence, describe the supplied story using character, setting and plot, explain two meanings of one word, and build a related word for a given context. Add a brief meaning or example beside each entry so a classmate could use it.
adjust: Starter: choose from the supplied meanings and explain one clue with an adult. Core: complete the four kinds of vocabulary use with your own clear sentences. Stretch: use plot in two topic contexts and explain how the surrounding words guide each interpretation.
safety: Read unfamiliar words aloud and give their meanings before asking learners to apply them. Use supplied measurements and fictional texts so specialist background knowledge is not required.
tricky: 1. Is setting only a place?
It includes where and when a story happens. Some texts tell both directly; others leave part unstated.
2. Does -ly always make a word mean the same thing?
It often helps describe how something is done, but real words need checking. Different and differently are related but work differently in sentences.
3. Does a context clue prove every possible meaning?
It supports the meaning that fits this passage. Another sentence may use the word in a different sense.
faq: What if I still cannot work out a word?
Ask a reader or use an age-appropriate dictionary, then reread the sentence with that meaning. A clue is a starting point, not a reason to guess forever.
Why learn vocabulary from different subjects?
Precise words help you explain learning: centimetre names a length unit and character names a story figure. Meaning still depends on use.
modelCaption: Keep the word connected to its sentence and purpose
